t:
(a) 
Section 2(b) of the National Housing Act is amended—

        (1) 
by striking out “$18,000 ($27,000 in the case of a mobile home containing two or more modules)” in the first sentence and inserting in lieu thereof “$20,000 ($30,000 in the case of a manufactured home composed of two or more modules)”;
 
        (2) 
by striking out subparagraph (A) of the second paragraph and inserting in lieu thereof the following:


“(A) 
involve an amount not exceeding $26,675 ($36,675 in the case of a manufactured home composed of more than two modules); and”;



 
        (3) 
by striking out subparagraph (A) of the third paragraph and inserting in lieu thereof the following:


“(A) 
involve an amount not exceeding $30,550 ($40,550 in the case of a manufactured home composed of two or more modules); and”; and



 
        (4) 
by striking out “$6,250 in the case of an undeveloped lot, or (ii) $9,375” in the fourth paragraph and inserting in lieu thereof “$6,950 in the case of an undeveloped lot, or (ii) $10,425”.
  
    (b) 
Section 2(b) of the National Housing Act is amended by adding the following new sentence at the end of the last paragraph: “In other areas where there are high land costs or high set-up costs, the Secretary may, by regulation, increase any such dollar amount limitation to—

        “(1) 
$32,500 (or $43,000 with respect to a manufactured home composed of two or more modules) in the case of a manufactured home and an undeveloped lot;
 
        “(2) 
$38,100 (or $49,000 with respect to a manufactured home composed of two or more modules) in the case of a manufactured home and a developed lot; and
 
        “(3) 
$11,750 (or $17,450 with respect to a developed lot) in the case of a lot in which to place a manufactured home.”.
  
    (c)
        (1) 
The National Housing Act is amended by striking out “mobile home” each place it appears and inserting in lieu thereof “manufactured home”.
 
        (2) Section 235(a)(2)(B) of such Act is amended by striking out “mobile homeowner” and “mobile homeowner’s” and inserting in lieu thereof “manufactured homeowner” and “manufactured home-owner’s”, respectively.
 
        (3) 
The United States Housing Act of 1937 is amended by striking out “mobile home” each place it appears and inserting in lieu thereof “manufactured home”.
 
        (4) 
Title VI of the Housing and Community Development Act of 1974 is amended by striking out “Mobile Home” each place it appears, other than in section 601, and inserting in lieu thereof “Manufactured Home” and by striking out “mobile home” each place it appears and inserting in lieu thereof “manufactured home”.
 
        (5) 
Section 601 of the Housing and Community Development Act of 1974 is amended by striking out “Mobile Home” and inserting in lieu thereof “Manufactured Housing”.
 
        (6) 
Section 501(e)(4) of Public Law 96–221 is amended by striking out “mobile home” and inserting in lieu thereof “manufactured home”.
 
        (7) 
In adopting regulations and procedures in accordance with this subsection, the Secretary of Housing and Urban Development shall have discretion to take actions in a manner which he deems necessary to insure that the public is fully aware of the distinctions between the various types of factory-built housing.
  
    (d) 
Section 603(6) of the Housing and Community Development Act of 1974 is amended—

        (A) 
by striking out “is eight body feet or more in width and is thirty-two body feet or more in length” and inserting in lieu thereof “, in the traveling mode, is eight body feet or more in width or forty body feet or more in length, or, when erected on site, is three hundred twenty or more square feet”; and
 
        (B) 
by inserting the following after the semicolon at the end thereof: “except that such term shall include any structure which meets all the requirements of this paragraph except the size requirements and with respect to which the manufacturer voluntarily files a certification required by the Secretary and complies with the standards established under this title;”.
  
    (e) 
Not later than January 1, 1982, the Secretary of Housing and Urban Development shall develop a procedure for collecting and regularly reporting data on the mean and median sales price for new manufactured homes, and, where available, data on the mean and median sales price for manufactured home lots and combination new manufactured home and lot packages. Such reports shall contain, to the maximum extent feasible, sales price information for the Nation, each census region, each State on an annual basis, and selected standard metropolitan statistical areas having sufficient activity on an annual basis.

fable.w: The tempting reading is that this section only amends dollar limits and swaps "mobile home" for "manufactured home", with no outside party named. However, subsection (b) authorizes the Secretary to raise the limits "by regulation", and under the definition a grant of rulemaking authority counts as participation even when it is discretionary ("may"), because rulemaking brings in public comment. Subsection (c)(7) also contemplates the Secretary "adopting regulations and procedures".
fable.s: the Secretary may, by regulation, increase any such dollar amount limitation

qwen_block.w: This section grants the Secretary the authority to issue regulations to adjust dollar amount limitations. According to the precedent in Example 6, when a statute gives a federal agency the authority to issue a regulation, it is considered participation, even if the authority is discretionary ('may'). This falls under the category of 'requiring rulemaking' or the broader interpretation that regulatory authority implies the procedural participation mechanisms associated with rulemaking.
qwen_block.s: the Secretary may, by regulation, increase any such dollar amount limitation
qwen_block.b:
Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that subsection (c)(7) involves participation because it requires the Secretary to take actions to ensure the "public is fully aware" of distinctions between housing types. However, this is a one-way communication (public awareness/education) rather than a two-way consultation or coordination where the public provides input into a decision. The definition requires the government to *consult* or *coordinate* with outsiders *before* making a decision. Merely informing the public does not constitute participation in the decision-making process. Furthermore, the primary content of the section is technical amendments to dollar limits and terminology, which are not participatory.

Another potential trap is subsection (b), which allows the Secretary to increase limits "by regulation." As seen in Example 6, the authority to issue regulations is sometimes labeled "Yes" in this dataset's logic because rulemaking often implies public comment periods. However, looking at the strict definition provided: "Participation is when the federal government may or must consult or coordinate with people outside of the government...". The text itself does not explicitly mandate consultation, comment periods, or hearings. It just grants authority. In Example 6, the justification was "When a statute gives a federal agency the authority to issue a regulation, we could that as participation." This is a specific, somewhat idiosyncratic rule in the examples. Let's re-read Example 6 carefully. It says "we could that as participation" (likely a typo for "count that"). But wait, Example 3 says consultation for a study is "No". Example 11 says an opportunity to present views in an enforcement context is "No".

Let's look at the "Yes" criteria again:
- requiring a public comment period, or requiring rulemaking;
- a public hearing or public meeting;
- an advisory committee...
- consultation or coordination with states...
- granting an outside party the right to sue...

Subsection (b) says "the Secretary may, by regulation, increase...". Does this *require* rulemaking? It authorizes it. The definition says "requiring rulemaking" is a Yes. Does "may by regulation" count as "requiring rulemaking"? Usually, "may" is discretionary. However, Example 6 explicitly states: "When a statute gives a federal agency the authority to issue a regulation, we could that as participation. We do this even when Congress gives the agency discretion... as signified by the with 'may' in this text."

So, based on Example 6, the grant of authority to issue regulations is considered "Yes".

Let's check if there are other parts. Subsection (c)(7) mentions the public, but as noted, it's about awareness, not consultation.

So the key is subsection (b). The Secretary is authorized to issue regulations. Per Example 6, this is "Yes".

opus.w: The section lets the Secretary of Housing and Urban Development raise the dollar limits by regulation. Under the definition, rulemaking counts as participation, and Example 6 labels an almost identical National Housing Act clause 'Yes' even though 'may' makes it optional. The tempting 'No' reading treats the section as nothing but dollar-amount changes and renaming, but it misses this rulemaking authority.
opus.s: In other areas where there are high land costs or high set-up costs, the Secretary may, by regulation, increase any such dollar amount limitation to—
opus.b:
I labelled this **Yes**, with fairly high confidence (0.8).

**Tempting-but-wrong reading:** Most of the section only changes dollar caps and swaps "mobile home" for "manufactured home." No advisory body, hearing or consultation with outsiders is named, so it looks like a plain "No."

**Why that fails:** Subsection (b) lets the Secretary raise the loan limits "by regulation." Under the definition, requiring rulemaking counts as participation, because rulemaking brings in public notice and comment. Example 6 sets the precedent: a nearly identical National Housing Act clause ("the Secretary may by regulation increase…") was labelled "Yes," even though "may" makes the rule optional. Subsection (c)(7), on "adopting regulations and procedures," supports the same reading.

qwen_chat.w: The section amends definitions, sets financial limits for housing programs, and requires the Secretary to collect and report data. It does not require consultation with, or coordination by, outside parties (such as the public, states, or experts) before making a decision. Subsection (c)(7) directs the Secretary to ensure the public is aware of distinctions, but this is an informational goal, not a participatory process. Subsection (b) grants authority to set limits by regulation but does not mandate a public comment period or consultation.
qwen_chat.b:
Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that subsection (c)(7) requires the Secretary to take actions to ensure the "public is fully aware," which sounds like public participation or outreach. However, this is an internal directive to the agency on how to frame its regulations and procedures, not a requirement to consult with or coordinate with the public before making a decision. The public is the recipient of information, not a participant in the decision-making process.

Another tempting reading is that the Secretary's authority to increase dollar limits "by regulation" in subsection (b) implies rulemaking, which often involves public comment. However, the text itself does not explicitly require a public comment period or consultation; it merely grants the authority to set limits. Without explicit language requiring public input (like "after notice and comment" or "consultation with..."), this is an exercise of agency discretion, not mandated participation.

The section primarily deals with amending definitions, setting financial limits, and requiring data collection and reporting. None of these actions involve consulting with or coordinating with outside parties (states, tribes, public, experts) before a federal decision is made. The reports in (e) are for data collection, not for public input.
